storyText:
Mina and Joon began their summer job at the Harbor Point Museum. Rain covered the windows, and the sea looked dark from the road. When the sky began to brighten up, Mr Han opened the main door. Mina and Joon carried boxes into the main room.

The museum was small, but it held the history of the town. An old metal lamp stood in a glass case by the stairs. Mr Han said the lamp once guided boats through storms. Joon began to perk up when he heard about the rescue boats.

Mina and Joon could get around the town on their bicycles. Their task was to go to local family homes and collect stories for a new show. They had two work forms to fill in. Mina wrote carefully, while Joon drew a tiny boat by his name.

Mr Han asked them to look over the lamp case. The lock was closed, but there was a thin line of sand in the glass. A card by the case said that the lamp had come from the signal house on the high hill. Mina saw that the date on the card was wrong.

The summer opening was only three days away. Red paint had begun to run out, and half the history wall was still empty. Mr Han tried to laugh about the work, but his face looked tired. Mina promised that she and Joon would finish the wall in time.


At the back of the lamp case, Mina found a narrow wooden box. Someone had tucked it away between the wall and a heavy shelf. The box held a weather notebook, a small key, and a map with one corner missing. The last page carried the name Leo Park.

Mina read the notebook twice, but she could not take in the ending message. It said that the lamp must return to the hill when the red storm flag rose. Joon wanted to show the notebook to Mr Han at once. Mina asked for one quiet hour to read the map.

Mr Han came into the room and saw the open box. He did not ask about the old place of the box. Instead, he began to open up about his father Leo, the man from the old signal house. After Leo was gone, Mr Han closed the house and never climbed the hill again.

Mina and Joon sat on the floor to think through the clues. The map showed a path from the museum to a spring at the back of the hill. A blue mark stood at the end of the old road. The missing corner probably held the signal house.

Joon felt that Mina had let him down by hiding the notebook for an hour. Mina said she had only wanted time to understand it. Their quiet talk ended when the radio gave a weather warning. A strong storm would reach Harbor Point in one day.


They began their walk early in the morning with the notebook, the key, and two raincoats. Mr Han agreed to follow after he closed the museum. The path crossed gardens and fields at the start. High on the hill, tall grass hid the old road.

At the spring, Mina and Joon set up a small shelter by a rock. They compared the notebook with the marks by the water. A narrow arrow pointed to a bridge at the cliff. Joon packed the map while Mina checked the weather.

The wooden bridge shook in the wind. A board moved when Joon stepped on it, and Mina told him to watch out. Joon stepped back and held the rope by the path. They crossed one at a time and did not look down.

After the bridge, they stopped to cool down in the shadow of a wall. Mina found the missing map corner between two flat rocks. It showed a new path that turned away from the cliff. The safe path was long, but the wind was growing strong.

They chose to push on by the safe path. A sudden wind lifted the map corner from Mina's hand. Joon ran through the grass and picked it up at the edge of the cliff. When he returned, Mina thanked him and gave him the full map.


The signal house stood by three bent trees. The roof was damaged, and one window had broken glass. When Joon touched the door, a loose board fell from the roof. Mina told him to back off until the dust was gone.

The small key opened the door, but the room was almost dark. White numbers covered one wall, and a metal wheel was by them. The notebook spelled out the order for turning the wheel. Mina read the steps slowly while Joon followed them.

The wheel stopped after three turns. A voice from the road called for them to hold on. Mr Han entered with a bag of tools and examined the old machine. He had followed their bicycle marks from the museum.

The three arrived at a simple answer. The machine was not a secret lock; it moved the great mirror on the roof. The museum lamp had once stood by that mirror. The signal needed the lamp to cross the water.

Mr Han wanted to bring in a machine expert from the town. The storm would arrive soon, so they checked over the wheel themselves. Joon made the metal clean, Mina copied the steps, and Mr Han fixed the broken handle. By evening, the mirror could move again.


The three returned to the museum as hard rain began. Mr Han opened the glass case and lifted the lamp from it. Mina carried it in her hands, and Joon protected the fire box from the rain. They climbed to the signal house again that day.

A rescue group had gone to care for two men on a fishing boat. The boat radio was weak, and the harbor light had lost power. Mr Han placed the lamp at the great mirror. Mina made the lamp burn while Joon turned the repaired wheel.

The light pointed into the dark sky. Joon moved the wheel one mark, and a wide line of light crossed the dark water. The fishing boat answered with a short light. The three in the signal house knew that the boat had seen them.

Mr Han watched over the lamp while Mina spoke to the harbor office by radio. Joon kept the mirror on the path between the boat and the safe water. Wind hit the roof, but the old house remained strong. At midnight, the rescue boat and the fishing boat entered the harbor.

When the storm ended, the room was quiet for a moment. Mr Han touched the notebook from his father and looked through the wet window. He said that Leo had prepared the signal house for a night like this. Mina understood that the notebook had waited at the back of the museum wall.


In the morning, Mina chose to own up to keeping the notebook from Joon and Mr Han. She explained that she had wanted to solve the mystery without sharing it. Joon admitted that he had been angry because he feared losing the chance to help. Mr Han listened without blaming them.

Mina and Joon talked out their problem on the museum steps. Mina promised to share important clues, and Joon promised to ask and not judge her quickly. They made up as the doors opened. Then they began the work on the history wall as a team.

Two days later, they heard from the captain of the fishing boat. He sent a picture of the light crossing the storm. The picture became the center of the new museum show. Mr Han placed Leo's notebook and the repaired map by it.

The lamp returned to the glass case, but the card now told the full story. Visitors could turn a model wheel and guide a small light across a painted sea. Children stayed to read the full notebook. The old signal house was remembered again.

On the final evening, the three examined the quiet room. The job had started out as three cards and a coat of paint. It had become a story about trust, memory, and a light shared in trouble. On the hill, the real lamp shone at Harbor Point.
